Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Dysphoria IoT Botnet Adds Blockchain C2 and Victim Relays After JackSkid Disruption

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Dysphoria, an Internet of Things (IoT) botnet line tracked by CNCERT and XLab, has adopted blockchain-based name services and infected-device relays after a March law-enforcement operation against JackSkid infrastructure. The researchers say the design makes the botnet harder to disrupt. CNCERT, China's national computer emergency response team, and XLab, the threat-intelligence lab of Chinese

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised device Telnet/SSH weak-password worm fan-out · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Dysphoria botnet blockchain C2 resolution via ENS/SNS (.eth/.sol) domains · [LLM] Egress to Dysphoria distribution-node / relay IPs (194.87.198.x, 194.58.38.x) · [LLM] Dysphoria relay node: public-to-public traffic bridging (UPnP port-forwarding relay) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Dysphoria botnet blockchain C2 resolution via ENS/SNS (.eth/.sol) domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the Dysphoria/JackSkid blockchain naming-service C2 records (m3rnbvs5d.eth, burrberry.eth, 24carnforth2merseyside.sol) or any .eth/.sol pseudo-TLD used to encode distribution-node IPv4 addresses. Blockchain name resolution on IoT/enterprise gear is highly abnormal and is the botnet's headline resilience mechanism. Rationale: Anchored on the three concrete blockchain C2 records named by XLab/CNCERT and cross-confirmed by BleepingComputer and GBHackers; .eth/.sol resolution is near-zero baseline on corporate/IoT segments, making the pseudo-TLD hunt high-fidelity as well as the exact-domain match. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1568 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web3/blockchain developer workstations resolving ENS/SNS names via eth.limo or eth.link gateways
  • MetaMask or other crypto wallet browser extensions performing ENS lookups
  • DeFi/NFT research or trading endpoints in fintech orgs
  • Security researchers detonating samples in an internal sandbox
  • IPFS gateways that proxy .eth content addresses
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and RemoteUrl has_any ("eth.limo","eth.link"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving asset — if it is an IoT device, router, camera or Linux edge box with no legitimate crypto function, treat as compromised; capture InitiatingProcess and the resolved IPv4. 2) Contain: block the .eth/.sol domains and any resolved distribution-node IPs at the egress firewall and isolate the device from the internet. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs (see distribution-node UC), search the same segment for Telnet/SSH scanning fan-out and UPnP port-mapping bursts, and sweep all IoT subnets for additional .eth/.sol resolvers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or RemoteUrl endswith ".eth" or RemoteUrl endswith ".sol"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol")
    or Name endswith ".eth" or Name endswith ".sol"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Answer = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria IoT Botnet Blockchain C2 Domain Resolution (ENS/SNS)
id: 9c1f2a44-7b3e-4c6a-9d21-8e5f0a3b1c77
description: Detects DNS resolution of Dysphoria/JackSkid blockchain naming-service C2 records or any .eth/.sol pseudo-TLD used to hide distribution-node IPv4 addresses.
references:

  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
author: SOC Detection Engineering

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query IN ("m3rnbvs5d.eth","burrberry.eth","24carnforth2merseyside.sol","*.eth","*.sol") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.answer DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Egress to Dysphoria distribution-node / relay IPs (194.87.198.x, 194.58.38.x) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any monitored host connecting to the five Dysphoria distribution-node IPv4 addresses that the ENS/SNS records resolve to and that infected relays forward traffic through. These are named campaign IOCs so a hit is high-confidence C2/relay activity. Rationale: The five IPs are the pre-extracted campaign IOCs and correspond to the HTTP-served distribution nodes/relays described by XLab (confirmed by GBHackers/BleepingComputer); a direct-IP match needs no behavioural context to be actionable. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) reaching the IPs during a scheduled scan
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing published IOCs
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where the address later serves a benign service
  • Security researcher sandbox traffic egressing through the corporate perimeter
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessusd","qualys-cloud-agent"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm direction and initiating process/asset; a low-privilege IoT/edge device beaconing to these IPs is a confirmed relay/bot. 2) Contain: block the five IPs at egress, quarantine the source device, and preserve any /tmp payloads for the malware team. 3) Hunt: correlate the source with .eth/.sol resolution and Telnet/SSH scanning UCs, and check whether the host is also serving inbound public connections (relay role).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Dysphoria Botnet Distribution-Node C2 IP Connection
id: 3a7d6e12-4f88-4b0c-a1e9-2c4b7f9d5e30
description: Detects outbound connections to the five Dysphoria/JackSkid distribution-node and relay IPv4 addresses published by XLab and CNCERT.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

      - '194.58.38.79'
      - '194.58.38.49'
      - '194.58.38.96'
  condition: selection

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:(194.87.198.208 OR 194.87.198.104 OR 194.58.38.79 OR 194.58.38.49 OR 194.58.38.96)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(194\.87\.198\.(208|104)|194\.58\.38\.(79|49|96))$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("194.87.198.208","194.87.198.104","194.58.38.79","194.58.38.49","194.58.38.96") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Compromised device Telnet/SSH weak-password worm fan-out AIDelivery Medium
Detects a single internal host initiating outbound connections to many distinct public destinations on TCP/23 (Telnet) or TCP/22 (SSH) — the credential-guessing worm-spread behaviour XLab and CNCERT call the botnet's most consistent way in. High distinct-destination fan-out on these ports is the signature of a newly infected node scanning for the next victim. Rationale: Both published lists agree weak Telnet/SSH credential guessing is the primary propagation channel; distinct-destination fan-out on 22/23 from one source is the cleanest network expression of that worm behaviour without needing per-device auth logs the IoT gear won't ship. Threshold is aggregation-based so no single-event Sigma is emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1021.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Nmap) sweeping SSH/Telnet across a range
  • Ansible/SaltStack/Puppet config-management pushing to many hosts over SSH
  • IT jump/bastion host with legitimate broad SSH reach
  • Network monitoring platform probing device availability on 22/23
  • Backup or patch-orchestration appliance connecting to many managed devices
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("bastion","jump","scanner","ansible","nessus","qualys") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nmap","nessusd","ssh","sshpass","ansible"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the source a sanctioned scanner/bastion/config-mgmt host? Check the initiating process and whether targets are internal (admin) or public (worm scan) — public fan-out from an IoT/edge device is malicious. 2) Contain: block outbound 22/23 from the device, isolate it, and rotate any credentials it could have brute-forced. 3) Hunt: check the same host for .eth/.sol resolution and distribution-node IP egress; sweep destinations it hit for successful logons indicating fresh compromise.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort in (22, 23)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), SampleTargets = make_set(RemoteIP, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets >= 30   // 30 = worm-scan fan-out floor; normal client SSH/Telnet hits <5 distinct public hosts/day
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 23)
| where CommunicationDirection =~ "Outbound" or isempty(CommunicationDirection)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationPort
| where DistinctTargets >= 30   // worm-scan fan-out floor
| order by DistinctTargets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(22 OR 23)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=22 OR RemotePort=23) ConnectionDirection=1
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count >= 30
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets >= 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (22,23) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where distinct_targets >= 30 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - distinct_targets
Dysphoria relay node: public-to-public traffic bridging (UPnP port-forwarding relay) AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the relay-only Dysphoria variant that drops DDoS modules and turns a device into a proxy, using UPnP to create ~155 gateway port-forwarding rules and Linux epoll to shuttle traffic between an inbound internet connection and a remote C2. Surfaces monitored hosts that simultaneously accept many inbound public connections and open many outbound public connections — the traffic-symmetry signature of a relay bridge. Rationale: Anchored on XLab's June relay-only variant that uses UPnP (155 port-forwarding rules, per BleepingComputer) and epoll to bridge an inbound internet connection to a remote C2; the detectable enterprise signature is one host with high inbound-public AND high outbound-public connection cardinality. Confidence is Low because IoT relays rarely emit EDR telemetry and legit reverse proxies share the shape — treat as a triage-list hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-dysphoria-ddos-botnet-spreads-to-200k-devices-worldwide/ • https://gbhackers.com/dysphoria-iot-botnet/
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate reverse proxies / load balancers (NGINX, HAProxy) fronting public services
  • VPN concentrators or SASE gateways terminating and forwarding sessions
  • Corporate NAT gateway or SD-WAN edge bridging many flows
  • Public-facing jump/bastion host with broad inbound and outbound reach
  • CDN or caching appliance in a DMZ
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("proxy","lb","haproxy","nginx","vpn","gateway","bastion","edge")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a sanctioned proxy/gateway/LB; an IoT device, camera, router or unmanaged Linux box exhibiting relay symmetry is suspect — inspect for miniupnpd/UPnP AddPortMapping bursts and unexpected listeners. 2) Contain: remove the device's UPnP port mappings on the gateway, block its inbound exposure, and isolate it. 3) Hunt: pivot the host's outbound peers against the distribution-node IP and .eth/.sol UCs, and enumerate the gateway for the ~155 forwarding rules characteristic of this variant.
let Window = 1d;
let Inbound = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize InboundPublic = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
let Outbound = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionRequest")
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize OutboundPublic = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId;
Inbound
| join kind=inner Outbound on DeviceId
| where InboundPublic >= 10 and OutboundPublic >= 10   // relay bridges public<->public on one node
| project DeviceName, InboundPublic, OutboundPublic
| order by InboundPublic desc
let Window = 1d;
let Inb = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where NetworkDirection =~ "Inbound"
    | where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == false
    | summarize InboundPublic = dcount(SrcIpAddr) by DvcHostname;
let Outb = ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where NetworkDirection =~ "Outbound"
    | where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
    | summarize OutboundPublic = dcount(DstIpAddr) by DvcHostname;
Inb
| join kind=inner Outb on DvcHostname
| where InboundPublic >= 10 and OutboundPublic >= 10
| project DvcHostname, InboundPublic, OutboundPublic
| order by InboundPublic desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=0 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(?!10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count >= 10
| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(?!10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.)/ | groupBy([aid], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true)) | _count >= 10}, field=aid)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.src_ip) as inbound_sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.dest_ip | rename All_Traffic.dest_ip as host | where inbound_sources >= 10 | append [| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as outbound_dests from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip | rename All_Traffic.src_ip as host | where outbound_dests >= 10] | stats values(inbound_sources) as inbound_sources values(outbound_dests) as outbound_dests by host | where isnotnull(inbound_sources) AND isnotnull(outbound_dests)
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.src_ip) as inbound_sources from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="inbound" by All_Traffic.dest_ip | rename All_Traffic.dest_ip as host | where inbound_sources >= 10 | append [| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as outbound_dests from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.src_ip | rename All_Traffic.src_ip as host | where outbound_dests >= 10] | stats values(inbound_sources) as inbound_sources values(outbound_dests) as outbound_dests by host | where isnotnull(inbound_sources) AND isnotnull(outbound_dests)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-9528")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-9528")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

tags:

detection:

            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Public Exploit Released for Patched vBulletin Pre-Auth Code Execution Flaw

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Public exploit details released on July 27 show how an unauthenticated request can reach PHP's eval() function inside vBulletin and execute code on an unpatched forum server. The attack requires no account, administrative access, or interaction from another user. SSD Secure Disclosure lists vBulletin 6.2.1 and earlier, and 6.1.6 and earlier, as affected, but does not give a lower version

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via operator-laden pagenav[pagenumber] to ajax/render/pagenav · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via operator-laden pagenav[pagenumber] to ajax/render/pagenav AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to vBulletin's public template-render route ajax/render/pagenav where the pagenav[pagenumber] parameter — normally a plain integer — carries parentheses, XOR/OR/NOT operators or concatenation characters. This is the exact 'phpfuck' restricted-character payload SSD's PoC feeds into vB5_Template_Runtime::runMaths() and PHP eval() for unauthenticated code execution. Rationale: pagenav[pagenumber] legitimately only ever holds an integer, so any parenthesis, XOR (^/%5e), OR (|/%7c), NOT (~/%7e) or concatenation character in it on the ajax/render/pagenav route is the phpfuck eval payload from SSD's PoC — near-zero legitimate overlap. Corroborated against SSD's technical advisory and independent write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners/pentest tools (Acunetix, Nuclei) firing the same CVE-2026-61511 template against your own forum
  • Internal vulnerability-management authenticated scans replaying the PoC
  • A plugin or theme that legitimately passes non-numeric pagenav values (rare — verify against a known-good baseline)
  • WAF in monitor-only mode logging blocked attempts that never reached PHP
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the endpoint from known IPs
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in ("blocked","deny","Blocked") and SourceIP !in ("")   // keep allowed requests; append known scanner IPs to the exclusion list
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL/body and SourceIP; URL-decode the pagenav[pagenumber] value and confirm it reconstructs PHP tokens (parentheses + ^ + digits, no letters). Check whether the WAF blocked or allowed (DeviceAction) and the HTTP response code. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, and confirm the forum is on vBulletin 6.2.2 (or branch patch for 6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6) — if not, take it offline or virtual-patch the ajax/render/pagenav route immediately. 3) Hunt: on the web host run the companion 'web-server spawns shell' detection to see if system() executed, review file writes under the webroot for dropped PHP web shells, and search all historical logs for the same SourceIP and payload signature.

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/httpd/w3wp) spawning OS shell — CVE-2026-61511 post-exploitation AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the vBulletin/PHP web-server process spawning a command interpreter or recon binary, which is exactly what SSD's PoC does after rebuilding PHP's system() to run an OS command and return output in the HTTP response. A php-fpm/httpd/w3wp parent launching cmd/powershell/bash/curl/whoami is not normal forum behaviour. Rationale: A php-fpm/httpd/w3wp/nginx parent process spawning cmd/powershell/bash/curl/whoami is the direct on-host artefact of the runMaths()->eval()->system() chain described by SSD; forum servers effectively never legitimately shell out from the web worker. Parent+child pairing keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP plugins that shell out (image processing via ImageMagick/convert, cron-like maintenance tasks)
  • Server admins running interactive troubleshooting under the web service account
  • Deployment/CI scripts invoking curl or git from the web root during releases
  • Monitoring agents that exec whoami/uname under the httpd context
  • Backup jobs spawned by the web user
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("convert","ImageMagick","git pull","/usr/local/bin/backup")   // drop known benign image/maintenance shell-outs; tune per environment
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine and grandparent chain; benign maintenance has predictable args (image resize, git pull) whereas exploitation shows recon (whoami/id/uname) or outbound curl/wget to unknown hosts. Correlate the timestamp with the web-log detection's SourceIP hitting ajax/render/pagenav. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and rotate any DB/API credentials readable from the vBulletin config. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web user under the webroot for PHP web shells, review outbound connections from the web-server process, and confirm patch level is 6.2.2.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-cgi","php","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","w3wp.exe","nginx","nginx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","dash","curl","curl.exe","wget","whoami","whoami.exe","id","uname","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Unpatched vBulletin instances exposed to CVE-2026-61511 AIReconnaissance Medium
Audit hunt surfacing managed hosts running vBulletin below the fixed 6.2.2 release (affected: 6.2.1 and earlier, 6.1.6 and earlier). Given a public exploit is live and the fix predates disclosure by ~4 weeks, this identifies the concentrated self-hosted, internet-facing population still exploitable. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete CVE id CVE-2026-61511 and the vendor's fixed version 6.2.2 versus affected 6.2.1/6.1.6-and-earlier stated in the article and SSD advisory; joining IsInternetFacing prioritises the exact exploitable population the article flags. If TVM has not yet mapped the CVE, fall back to DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory where SoftwareName has 'vbulletin' and SoftwareVersion != '6.2.2'. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://gbhackers.com/vbulletin-pre-auth-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 6.2.2 but TVM inventory lagging its scan refresh
  • Development/staging forum clones not reachable from the internet (lower priority, not false — still vulnerable)
  • vBulletin Cloud-managed sites reported already patched by the vendor
  • Version string parsed from a customised/rebranded footer that misreports the build
  • Decommissioned hosts still in the TVM inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: sort results by IsInternetFacing to prioritise externally reachable forums; confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below 6.2.2 (or a branch patch for 6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6). 2) Contain: schedule emergency upgrade to 6.2.2 or apply the branch patch; where patching is delayed, virtual-patch or block the ajax/render/pagenav route at the WAF. 3) Hunt: for each unpatched internet-facing host, run the web-log payload detection and the web-server-spawns-shell detection over the full ~4-week exposure window (late-June patch to July-27 disclosure) to check for prior compromise.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"

Critical

n8n Sandbox Escape Lets Workflow Editors Run OS Commands as the n8n Process

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 10 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

n8n has patched a high-severity expression-sandbox escape that could let an authenticated workflow editor execute operating-system commands on the server running the automation platform. Security Joes found the flaw while probing n8n's February fix for CVE-2026-27577 for another bypass. The affected ranges are &lt;2.31.5 and &gt;=2.32.0,&lt;2.32.1. n8n fixed the flaw in versions 2.31.5 and

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] n8n/Node.js process spawning shell or recon utility (sandbox-escape RCE) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — n8n Sandbox Escape Lets Workflow Editors Run OS Commands as the n8n Process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] curl/wget/nc spawned by n8n/Node reaching external hosts (post-escape C2/exfil)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] n8n/Node child command accessing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host credential stores
n8n/Node.js process spawning shell or recon utility (sandbox-escape RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the direct observable of the n8n expression-sandbox escape (GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m): the n8n/Node process loading child_process and executing OS commands, surfacing as a shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell) or recon utility (whoami/id/curl) spawned as a child of node/n8n. This is exactly the parent→child chain the advisory tells defenders to hunt. Rationale: Anchored on the advisory's explicit hunt guidance ('shells, PowerShell, curl, or wget spawned as children of the n8n or Node.js process') and the child_process load in the exploit chain; parent=node/n8n + shell/recon child is the escape's only host-level footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vpcf-gvg4-6qwr
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate n8n Execute Command node running sh/bash by design
  • Node-based CI runners or container entrypoints invoking bash/sh
  • Health-check workflows calling curl/wget to internal APIs
  • Admin debugging inside the n8n container (id/whoami)
  • Task-runner or npm lifecycle scripts spawning shell wrappers
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("n8n-nodes-base.executeCommand","/opt/n8n/healthcheck") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and the initiating node/n8n cmdline; confirm whether an Execute Command node exists in the workflow that ran, and identify the workflow author. 2) Contain: if the command is unexpected (recon, encryption-key read, outbound tooling), isolate the host and suspend the n8n workflow-editor account that authored/last-modified the workflow. 3) Hunt: review recently created/modified workflows for arrow functions or obfuscated JS, pivot on the same host for outbound connections and N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY access; rotate n8n credentials and the encryption key.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","n8n") or ParentProcessName has_any ("node","n8n")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","/pwsh","pwsh.exe","/whoami","/id","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/netcat","/python","/perl","/ruby")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: n8n Node.js Process Spawning Shell or Recon Utility (Sandbox Escape)
id: 3c9d1e6a-8b42-4f21-9d7a-1f2b6c4e8a01
status: experimental
description: Detects n8n/Node.js spawning a command interpreter or recon utility, the direct observable of the n8n expression-sandbox escape GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m (child_process RCE).
references:
  - https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/node'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/n8n'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/ksh'
      - '/csh'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '/pwsh'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/id'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/netcat'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/ruby'
  condition: parent and child
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate n8n Execute Command node usage
  - CI/CD or container entrypoint scripts launched by node
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\n8n.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\nc.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|n8n)(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/[\/\\](sh|bash|dash|zsh|ksh|csh|cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|pwsh|whoami|id|curl|wget|nc|ncat|netcat|python3?|perl|ruby)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node","node.exe","n8n")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","csh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","pwsh.exe","whoami","id","curl","wget","nc","ncat","netcat","python","python3","perl","ruby")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
curl/wget/nc spawned by n8n/Node reaching external hosts (post-escape C2/exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress originating from a download/transfer utility (curl, wget, nc, python) whose parent is the n8n/Node process — the payload-fetch or exfil step after the sandbox escape. Distinct from the process-spawn UC by pivoting on the outbound public connection rather than the spawn event. Rationale: The advisory names curl/wget as children to hunt, and Security Joes notes the escape opens 'paths to connected databases, internal services, and cloud endpoints' — a transfer utility parented by node reaching a public IP is the payload-fetch/exfil observable. Sentinel/Splunk express it via process telemetry since ASIM/CIM network events aren't parent-attributed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n HTTP Request node internally shelling out to curl for an integration
  • Workflow that legitimately fetches files from a public API via curl/wget
  • Python-based custom n8n node calling external SaaS endpoints
  • Container image pulls or update scripts run under the node parent
  • Monitoring/health probes to external status pages
Suppression filter
| where RemotePort in (4444,5555,6666,7777,8888,9999) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","netcat")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and the utility's full command line; check whether the destination matches a known integration endpoint for that workflow. 2) Contain: block the destination at egress and isolate the host if the destination is unrecognized or the transfer is credential-bearing. 3) Hunt: correlate to the process-spawn UC on the same host/time, review the responsible workflow for arrow-function/obfuscated JS, and rotate any credentials reachable from the n8n host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

n8n/Node child command accessing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host credential stores AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts commands spawned under the n8n/Node process that read the n8n encryption key, host secret files (/etc/shadow, SSH keys, cloud creds) or dump the environment — the credential-theft objective Security Joes flagged (exposing N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY to decrypt stored credentials). Pivots on command-line content rather than the child binary name. Rationale: Directly anchored on Security Joes' finding that the escape 'could expose N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY and allow decryption of credentials stored in n8n'; a node-parented command touching that key or host secret files is high-fidelity credential access with almost no benign analogue. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/security/advisories/GHSA-gv7g-jm28-cr3m • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/n8n-sandbox-escape-lets-workflow.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • n8n startup legitimately reading its own .n8n/config file
  • Container init reading /proc/self/environ for config bootstrap
  • Admin running printenv inside the n8n container for troubleshooting
  • Backup jobs archiving the .n8n directory
  • Legit workflow that references an SSH key path for an SFTP integration
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has ".n8n/config" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "n8n start")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child command line and confirm whether it reads N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY or host secrets outside n8n's normal config load; identify the workflow and its author. 2) Contain: treat the encryption key and all n8n-stored credentials as compromised — rotate the key and every stored credential, and disable the responsible workflow-editor account. 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the host (exfil of the harvested secrets), review connected databases/cloud endpoints for the n8n service identity's activity, and audit other recently modified workflows for arrow-function/obfuscated JS.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node","node.exe","n8n")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY","/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","id_rsa",".aws/credentials",".n8n/config","printenv","/proc/self/environ",".ssh/","/root/.n8n")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","n8n") or ParentProcessName has_any ("node","n8n")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY","/etc/shadow","/etc/passwd","id_rsa",".aws/credentials",".n8n/config","printenv","/proc/self/environ",".ssh/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Operation BlueDash Deploys Level RMM and ScreenConnect via Fake Teams Update

The Hacker News
2026-07-27 16 use cases 8 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a Microsoft Teams-themed phishing campaign that employs "secure document" lures to deliver legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools. "The victim was directed through compromised web infrastructure to a counterfeit Microsoft Store page claiming that Microsoft Teams had to be updated before the shared document could be opened," ZeroBEC said in

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Operation BlueDash fake Teams/Zoom update payload-host infrastructure contact · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Operation BlueDash Deploys Level RMM and ScreenConnect via Fake Teams Update
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] supportdev.exe Inno Setup loader spawning hidden-window PowerShell · [LLM] Level RMM enrollment with BlueDash attacker API key (GxSCHE8EZwfyYN3iPQHPai8D) · [LLM] Multiple RMM agents co-resident on one host (BlueDash redundant access) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Host reconnaissance sequence spawned from an RMM agent context (BlueDash operator checklist) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Operation BlueDash fake Teams/Zoom update payload-host infrastructure contact AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact to the counterfeit Microsoft Store / GitHub Pages infrastructure used by Operation BlueDash to serve the fake Teams update and the supportdev.exe loader. These are hard campaign IOCs (teamvem.com, support.berrydev.xyz, berry4603.github.io) rather than generic phishing domains. Rationale: Uses the three confirmed BlueDash hostnames from the article body (teamvem.com fake Teams store page, support.berrydev.xyz actor infra, berry4603.github.io repo host) plus the pre-extracted anuyotindustries.com. Domain-exact matches make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/03/signed-malware-impersonating-workplace-apps-deploys-rmm-backdoors/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox reaching the live domain
  • Proxy/DNS sinkhole appliance pre-resolving IOC lists for blocking
  • github.io is shared infrastructure — only berry4603.github.io is malicious, a typo/partial match could catch other github.io if the has_any list is widened
  • Corporate phishing-simulation vendor mimicking the lure
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which host/user resolved the domain and whether supportdev.exe was subsequently written or executed (pivot to UC2). 2) Contain: block all four domains at proxy/DNS, isolate the host if a download or process launch followed the DNS hit. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for supportdev.exe file writes and any process command line containing LEVEL_API_KEY (UC3) or ScreenConnect/Tactical RMM installers landing in %TEMP%.

supportdev.exe Inno Setup loader spawning hidden-window PowerShell AIInstallation High
Detects the BlueDash first-stage loader supportdev.exe launching PowerShell in a hidden window to fetch and enroll RMM agents. The parent binary name plus the hidden-window child is the article's specific execution fingerprint. Rationale: supportdev.exe is the named Inno Setup loader from the article; pairing its unusual parent role with a hidden PowerShell child that pulls RMM installers is the exact execution behaviour ZeroBEC described. Parent-name match alone is near-unique. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/operation-bluedash-deploys-level-rmm.html • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/phishing-rmm-tools/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1564.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally named supportdev.exe run by a developer
  • Software-packaging QA testing an Inno Setup installer that shells PowerShell
  • EDR/AV sandbox replay of the sample generating benign telemetry
  • IT deployment script legitimately named support*.exe (widen-match risk if endswith is loosened)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\program files\", @"\programdata\microsoft\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full PowerShell command line and any child network connections — confirm whether it fetched a Level/ScreenConnect installer or referenced LEVEL_API_KEY. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the powershell process tree, and quarantine supportdev.exe (capture SHA256). 3) Hunt: search the same host and org for the enrollment key (UC3), co-resident RMM agents (UC4), and RMM-spawned recon (UC5).
DeviceProcessEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "supportdev.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| extend Cmd = tolower(ProcessCommandLine)
| where Cmd has_any ("-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","-win h"," hidden") or Cmd has_any ("downloadstring","invoke-webrequest","iwr","level_api_key")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\supportdev.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("hidden","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","LEVEL_API_KEY")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
